title: Who Gets Immunized: K After D, Duffy-Null Red Cells and FNAIT
summary: Rank the most immunogenic red cell antigens (D, then K) and know why rankings are estimates, explain the Duffy-null phenotype and its partial protection against Plasmodium vivax, and recognise and manage fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia, including in a first pregnancy.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 40 Hit 25 (immunogenicity ranking: D, then K), Hit 6 (Duffy-negative Fy(a−b−) cells and Plasmodium vivax), Hit 11 (FNAIT: anti-HPA-1a, incidence, treatment) and Hit 24 (FNAIT in a first pregnancy). Checked against Tiller 2017 (FNAIT review), Chung 2023 (limits of immunogenicity formulas), Aloshaywan 2026 and Makroo 2016 (K second only to D), Linder 2021 and Ares 2024 (Rh and Kell immunogenicity), Howes 2011 (global Duffy map), Zimmerman 2017 (vivax in Duffy-negative people) and Höher 2018 (Duffy molecular basis; read via a page-fetch tool because Europe PMC and the NCBI BioC API returned no full text). Qualified: Duffy-negative cells are resistant, not immune, to vivax; most HPA-1a immunizations in prospective studies occurred after delivery; neonatal FNAIT is treated first with platelet transfusion, IVIg being supplemental; HPA-1 share given as 80–90% in Caucasians by Tiller 2017. Pending, not taught: the full order D > K > C > E > Fya > c > Jka and the relative potencies 0.70/0.10; “68% of Black individuals”; HPA-1a share of 70–85%; severe disease (<25,000/μL) at 1:10,000.

objectives: Define immunogenicity, state that K ranks second only to D, and explain why published rankings and potency numbers vary.
Explain the cause of the Duffy-null phenotype in people of African ancestry and its partial protection against Plasmodium vivax.
Recognise FNAIT, its common HPA targets and first-pregnancy presentation, and outline neonatal and antenatal management.

scenes.title: Three antigens, three questions
scenes.altText: Invented scenario with three cards: (1) a K-negative patient is about to receive a K-positive unit; (2) a blood donor of West African ancestry types Fy(a−b−); (3) a healthy first-time mother whose term newborn has petechiae and a platelet count of 18 × 10⁹/L, with a normal maternal count. Question token: “Who makes antibody, who resists, and who is at risk?”

cues.text: Invented case one: a K-negative patient is about to receive K-positive red cells. How likely is an antibody?
Case two: a donor of West African ancestry types Duffy-negative, Fy a-minus b-minus. Is this donor protected from malaria?
Case three: a healthy first-time mother delivers a term baby with petechiae and a platelet count of eighteen thousand. Can a first pregnancy cause this?

props.label: Who makes antibody, who resists, who is at risk?

scenes.title: Immunogenicity: D first, then K
scenes.altText: Card 1: immunogenicity is the chance that an antigen-negative person exposed to antigen-positive cells makes the antibody. The classic estimate (Giblett): antibody frequency = p (antigen-positive donors) × q (antigen-negative recipients) × Im (immunogenicity). Card 2: D is the most immunogenic antigen outside ABO; up to about 80% of D-negative people exposed to D-positive red cells form anti-D. Card 3: K (KEL1) ranks second only to D. Card 4: Rh (C, E) and Kell (K) antigens are among the most immunogenic; anti-C, anti-E and anti-K historically made up to two-thirds of alloantibodies in sickle cell disease. ABO antibodies form without exposure, so ABO is a separate case.

cues.text: Immunogenicity is the chance that an antigen-negative person, exposed to antigen-positive red cells, makes the matching antibody. The classic estimate multiplies how often donors carry the antigen, how often recipients lack it, and an immunogenicity factor.
Outside ABO, D is the most immunogenic antigen: up to about eighty percent of D-negative people exposed to D-positive cells form anti-D.
The K antigen of the Kell system ranks second only to D. That is why the K-negative patient in case one is at real risk.

Rh antigens such as C and E, and Kell K, are among the most immunogenic; in sickle cell disease they historically caused up to two thirds of alloantibodies. ABO antibodies are different: they form without any exposure.

scenes.title: Duffy-null: a door shut on red cells only
scenes.altText: Card 1: the Duffy glycoprotein carries Fya or Fyb; the Fy(a−b−) phenotype is very common in sub-Saharan Africa (median 98–100% across western, central and south-eastern regions in a global map) and rare in Europeans. Card 2: in people of African ancestry it is caused by a GATA-1 binding-site variant in the FY*B promoter, which silences Duffy only in red cells; other tissues still express Fyb, so these people rarely make anti-Fyb. Card 3: P. vivax uses the Duffy antigen to invade red cells, so Duffy-negative cells are refractory and the phenotype generally confers resistance. Card 4: since about 2006, PCR studies have found P. vivax infection in Duffy-negative people across Africa and in South America: resistant, not malaria-proof.

cues.text: The Duffy protein carries the Fy a or Fy b antigen. The Duffy-null phenotype, Fy a-minus b-minus, is very common in sub-Saharan Africa, near one hundred percent in much of the west, centre and south-east, and rare in Europeans.

In people of African ancestry, a promoter variant breaks a binding site for the erythroid factor GATA-1. Duffy is silenced only in red cells; other tissues still make Fy b, so these people rarely form anti-Fy b.
Plasmodium vivax uses the Duffy antigen to enter red cells, so Duffy-negative cells are refractory to invasion. That is the textbook link between this phenotype and malaria resistance.

But resistance is not immunity. Molecular studies across Africa and in South America have found vivax infections in Duffy-negative people. The answer to case two: protected against vivax, not malaria-proof.

scenes.title: FNAIT: the platelet counterpart
scenes.altText: Card 1: FNAIT = maternal IgG against a fetal platelet antigen (HPA) that the mother lacks; about 1 per 1,000 births in Caucasian populations. HPA-1a sits on integrin β3 (GPIIIa); about 2% of Caucasian women are HPA-1a negative (HPA-1bb). HPA-1 causes 80–90% of Caucasian cases; anti-HPA-5b 7–16% and anti-HPA-15b 2–4%; HPA-4 and HPA-5 lead in Japanese patients. Card 2: intracranial hemorrhage about 1 in 10,000 births; most reported ICH cases are first-born children, yet prospective screening found more than 75% of HPA-1a immunizations happened after delivery. Card 3: lab: antibody detection by MAIPA (gold standard); diagnosis needs a fetal antigen the mother lacks plus maternal antibody. Card 4: newborn: platelet transfusion on clinical suspicion, HPA-compatible preferred, random-donor if unavailable, IVIg as a supplement; next pregnancy: weekly maternal IVIg from the second trimester when risk is high.

cues.text: Fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia is the platelet version of hemolytic disease: maternal IgG against a platelet antigen the fetus inherited from the father. In Caucasian populations, HPA-1a causes eighty to ninety percent of cases; HPA-5b and HPA-15b cause most of the rest.

It occurs in about one per thousand births, with intracranial hemorrhage in about one per ten thousand. Most reported hemorrhages are in first-born children, so case three fits. But prospective screening found that most HPA-1a immunizations happen after delivery.
In the lab, maternal platelet antibodies are detected with the MAIPA assay. The diagnosis needs a fetal platelet antigen the mother lacks, plus her matching antibody.

For the newborn, transfuse platelets as soon as FNAIT is suspected: HPA-compatible if available, random-donor if not, with IVIg as a supplement. In the next pregnancy, weekly maternal IVIg is the usual first-line therapy.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Duffy-negative means malaria-proof” (✓ resistant to vivax invasion, but vivax infections are documented); “FNAIT needs a sensitizing earlier pregnancy” (✓ first-born babies are often affected, although many HPA-1a immunizations occur at delivery); “Treat the FNAIT newborn with IVIg alone” (✓ platelet transfusion on suspicion, HPA-compatible preferred; IVIg is supplemental).

cues.text: Trap one: Duffy-negative means malaria-proof. No: Duffy-negative cells resist vivax invasion, but vivax infections in Duffy-negative people are documented.
Trap two: FNAIT cannot happen in a first pregnancy. It can, and first-born babies are often affected, unlike classic anti-D disease, even though many HPA-1a immunizations happen at delivery.
Trap three: treat the bleeding-risk newborn with IVIg alone. Platelets come first, given on suspicion and HPA-compatible when possible; IVIg is a supplement.

scenes.title: D then K, shut door, first-born platelets
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “D then K; Duffy shuts the door; platelets do not wait for baby two.” Tokens: D then K = immunogenicity order · Shut door = Fy(a−b−) resists vivax · Baby one = FNAIT can hit the first-born. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: D then K, Duffy shuts the door, and platelets do not wait for baby two. D and K head the immunogenicity list, Duffy-null cells shut vivax out, and FNAIT can strike a first-born.

Where it breaks: rankings are estimates that vary by method and population; the Duffy door is shut, not locked, since vivax still gets in sometimes; and most HPA-1a immunizations still happen around delivery.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “D first, K second · Duffy-null resists vivax, not immune”, “FNAIT can hit baby one → platelets on suspicion”.

cues.text: After D the K antigen is the most immunogenic, Duffy-null red cells resist but do not fully block Plasmodium vivax, and fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia from anti-HPA-1a can strike a first-born baby, who needs platelets as soon as it is suspected.

props.label: D first, K second · Duffy-null resists vivax, not immune
FNAIT can hit baby one → platelets on suspicion

explanation.what: Plain language: some red cell antigens are much more likely than others to make a person who lacks them produce an antibody; D comes first and K second. Some people of African ancestry have red cells without the Duffy protein, which makes it hard (but not impossible) for one malaria parasite to enter. And a mother can make antibodies against her baby’s platelets, sometimes in the very first pregnancy, causing dangerous bleeding. Scientific terms: immunogenicity, Giblett formula, RhD, Kell (K, KEL1), extended antigen matching, Duffy (Fya, Fyb, Fy(a−b−)), GATA-1 promoter variant, Plasmodium vivax, Duffy antigen receptor for chemokines, fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (FNAIT), human platelet antigen (HPA-1a, HPA-5b, HPA-15b), integrin β3, MAIPA, intracranial hemorrhage, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg).
explanation.why: An antibody forms only when an antigen-negative person meets antigen-positive cells, so observed antibody frequency depends on antigen frequency in donors and recipients as well as on immunogenicity itself. In Duffy-null people of African ancestry, a promoter variant blocks GATA-1 binding, silencing Duffy on red cells while other tissues keep Fyb; vivax needs Duffy to invade red cells. In FNAIT, maternal IgG against a paternally inherited platelet antigen crosses the placenta and fetal platelets are removed by phagocytosis.
explanation.measure: Immunogenicity estimate: antibody frequency = p × q × Im; up to ~80% of exposed D-negative people form anti-D; K second only to D. Fy(a−b−): median 98–100% across western, central and south-eastern Africa; rare in Europeans. FNAIT: ~1 per 1,000 births (Caucasian); ICH ~1 per 10,000 births; HPA-1 80–90% of Caucasian cases, HPA-5b 7–16%, HPA-15b 2–4%; ~2% of Caucasian women HPA-1a negative; MAIPA gold standard. Newborn: platelets on suspicion, HPA-compatible preferred, random-donor if unavailable, IVIg supplemental; subsequent pregnancy: weekly maternal IVIg from the second trimester when risk is high.
explanation.differs: FNAIT vs HDFN: platelets vs red cells; FNAIT frequently presents in a first-born, whereas anti-D HDFN classically follows sensitization at an earlier delivery. Duffy-null of African ancestry (red-cell-only silencing, rarely anti-Fyb) vs rare coding-region Duffy nulls in Europeans and Asians (at risk of Duffy alloimmunization). Immunogenicity ranking vs clinical significance: an antigen can be immunogenic and also cause severe disease (K), or be common in antibody files simply because it is often mismatched.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: which antigen is most immunogenic after D (K), why Duffy-negative people resist vivax, which platelet antigen causes most FNAIT in Caucasians (HPA-1a), whether FNAIT can occur in a first pregnancy (yes), and the first treatment for a severely thrombocytopenic FNAIT newborn (platelet transfusion).

comparisons.distinguisher: Which fetal cell the maternal IgG targets: an isolated low platelet count in a well baby points to FNAIT.

mnemonic.text: D then K; Duffy shuts the door; platelets do not wait for baby two.
mnemonic.explanation: D and K head the immunogenicity list; Duffy-null red cells shut Plasmodium vivax out; FNAIT can strike the first-born.
mnemonic.limitation: Rankings and potency numbers are estimates that vary by method and population; the Duffy door is shut, not locked (vivax infections in Duffy-negative people are documented); most HPA-1a immunizations in prospective studies occurred around delivery.

analogyLimitations: “Shut door” overstates protection: Duffy-negative people can be infected with vivax.
takeaway: After D the K antigen is the most immunogenic, Duffy-null red cells resist but do not fully block Plasmodium vivax, and fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia from anti-HPA-1a can strike a first-born baby, who needs platelets as soon as it is suspected.

questions.stem: A K-negative patient is to receive red cells. Apart from ABO and D, which antigen mismatch carries the highest risk of alloimmunization?

options.rationale: Correct. K is ranked second only to D in immunogenicity, so a K-negative recipient exposed to K-positive cells is at real risk of anti-K.
Incorrect. Fya ranks below K; K is the antigen ranked second only to D.
Incorrect. Jka is not the antigen ranked second to D; that position belongs to K.
Incorrect. M is not among the leading immunogenic antigens; Rh and Kell antigens lead the list.

questions.stem: A healthy term newborn of a first-time mother has widespread petechiae and a platelet count of 18 × 10⁹/L. The mother is well with a normal platelet count. FNAIT is suspected. What is the best immediate management?

options.text: Transfuse platelets now, HPA-compatible if available or random-donor if not
options.rationale: Correct. Correcting severe thrombocytopenia is a neonatal emergency; transfuse on clinical suspicion without waiting for confirmation, preferring HPA-compatible platelets.

options.text: Wait for MAIPA confirmation of maternal anti-HPA-1a before any treatment
options.rationale: Incorrect. Treatment should not await laboratory confirmation when the newborn is at risk of bleeding.

options.text: Rule out FNAIT because this is the mother’s first pregnancy
options.rationale: Incorrect. FNAIT often presents in a first-born child; most reported intracranial hemorrhages are in first-born babies.

options.text: Give IVIg alone and avoid platelet transfusion
options.rationale: Incorrect. IVIg is a supplemental therapy for the newborn; platelet transfusion is the first step.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Fy(a−b−) phenotype in people of West African ancestry is correct?

options.text: A promoter variant silences Duffy on red cells only; these people rarely make anti-Fyb, and their red cells resist, but do not fully block, Plasmodium vivax
options.rationale: Correct. The GATA-1 binding-site variant is red-cell-specific, other tissues still express Fyb, and vivax infections in Duffy-negative people have been documented.

options.text: Their red cells are completely immune to every malaria species
options.rationale: Incorrect. The Duffy link is to Plasmodium vivax (and P. knowlesi) invasion, and even vivax infection has been found in Duffy-negative people.

options.text: The phenotype is about as common in Europeans as in West Africans
options.rationale: Incorrect. It is very common in sub-Saharan Africa and rare in Europeans, where it comes from rare coding-region mutations.

options.text: They lack Duffy protein in every tissue and commonly form anti-Fyb after transfusion
options.rationale: Incorrect. Silencing is red-cell-specific, so Fyb is still expressed elsewhere and anti-Fyb is rare.

claims.text: Immunogenicity estimate Ab = p × q × Im; published rankings inconsistent and population-dependent.
D most immunogenic outside ABO (up to ~80% of exposed D-negative form anti-D); K second only to D.
Rh and Kell antigens among the most immunogenic; anti-C, -E, -K up to two-thirds of SCD alloantibodies; ABO antibodies need no exposure.
Fy(a−b−) very common in sub-Saharan Africa (median 98–100% in much of it) and rare in Europeans.
GATA-1 promoter variant silences Duffy on red cells only; these people rarely make anti-Fyb.
Duffy-negative red cells refractory to vivax; vivax infections in Duffy-negative people documented in Africa and South America.
FNAIT mechanism, incidence ~1/1,000, HPA-1 80–90% (Caucasian), HPA-5b and HPA-15b, ICH ~1/10,000, MAIPA.
Most reported FNAIT ICH in first-born; prospective data show >75% of HPA-1a immunizations after delivery.
Neonatal platelet transfusion on suspicion (compatible preferred, random if unavailable), IVIg supplemental; weekly maternal IVIg in subsequent pregnancies.
Reviewer Hit 25: full order D > K > C > E > Fya > c > Jka with relative potencies 0.70 (D) and 0.10 (K).

claims.text: “D then K; Duffy shuts the door; platelets do not wait for baby two.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 40 Hit 6 (and the Memory Hook “Duffy-negative = malaria-proof (against vivax)”) presents Duffy negativity as full protection. Howes 2011, Zimmerman 2017 and Höher 2018 report P. vivax infections in Duffy-negative people across Africa and in South America; the phenotype generally confers resistance, not immunity. The “68% of Black individuals” figure was not verified (Höher 2018 gives >80% in African Americans). The lesson teaches resistance, not immunity (register flag rv-duffy-vivax-not-absolute).

Ch. 40 Hit 24 says FNAIT needs no prior sensitization. Tiller 2017: most reported ICH cases are first-born, but prospective screening studies found >75% of HPA-1a immunizations occurred after delivery (immunization during first pregnancies 4% and 24% in two other cohorts), so FNAIT pathophysiology is more like HDFN than previously thought. The lesson teaches both points (register flag rv-fnait-first-pregnancy-immunization).

Ch. 40 Hit 11 says “treat with IVIg” and gives HPA-1a as 70–85% with severe disease at 1:10,000. Tiller 2017: the affected newborn is treated first with platelet transfusion on suspicion (HPA-compatible preferred, random-donor if unavailable), IVIg being supplemental; weekly maternal IVIg is the antenatal therapy for later pregnancies; HPA-1 accounts for 80–90% of Caucasian cases and ICH occurs in ~1 per 10,000 births. The lesson teaches these (register flag rv-fnait-treatment-platelets-first).

Ch. 40 Hit 25 gives a fixed order (D > K > C > E > Fya > c > Jka) and relative potencies (0.70, 0.10). Chung 2023: immunogenicity estimates from antigen/antibody frequencies are retrospective, inconsistent between studies and affected by antigen frequency, repeated transfusion, antigen density and small numbers; K and Fya appear low in an Asian estimate. D first and K second are supported (Aloshaywan 2026, Makroo 2016); the rest of the order and the numbers are pending (register flag rv-immunogenicity-ranking-estimates).

verification.notes: All taught factual claims (9) checked against Tiller 2017, Chung 2023, Aloshaywan 2026, Makroo 2016, Linder 2021, Ares 2024, Howes 2011, Zimmerman 2017 and Höher 2018 (read via a page-fetch tool). Three reviewer claims (full ranking and potency numbers; 68% Duffy-null; 70–85% HPA-1a and severe-disease rate) are pending and not taught. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
